answer.evidence: The top kasagi has a light band at rows 1-2 and a lighter front-edge line at row 3, followed by dark eave shadow at rows 4-5. That meets evidence (a), so it reads as a thin top slope, 3 rows of top surface. Below it the gate is all front-facing. The shimaki at rows 7-8 and the nuki at rows 9-14 are flat vertical strips with no top surface. The pillars at rows 15-24 and the stone bases at rows 24-30 are vertical faces with at most a 1-2 row lip. Because the beams show no top, not all major parts have a top surface.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate is a small torii gate, much smaller and simpler than the whole-building references. The measured facts are close to the references: 11 visible tones per tile against 12 and 10, 0% near-flat coverage, and 0% neutral dark edge pixels, so the outline is tinted dark red-brown rather than black. By eye, though, each red pillar and the two kasagi beams show only about 3 lightness steps (highlight, mid red, dark red) with little grain or per-element texture. The stone bases are similarly shallow. The references carry 5-6 steps per material, per-tile scallops and plaster or stone speckle. The measured tone count probably overstates the visible richness, since it counts the many small areas of the multi-part structure. The candidate looks thinner and flatter than the references, closer to a clean icon than a Beodeul-grade prop. With no texture dots on the posts or beams, I cannot say a careful artist would accept it next to the references.

answer.evidence: The kasagi at the top (rows 1-3) is a blue-gray band that ends in a lighter front-edge line at row 3. Dark eave shadow follows in rows 4-5, so it reads as a roof top surface of about 3 rows. Below it the red shimaki (rows 7-8), nuki (rows 9-13), pillars (rows 15-24) and stone bases (rows 25-30) form a vertical front face of about 24 rows. The beams and pillars are vertical faces with no side face drawn. The stone bases show only a 2-row light strip at rows 26-27, which is a rim at most.

styleAnswer.evidence: The torii is a thin, sparse prop set against two full houses, so I judged mostly by eye. The measured facts are not against it: 11 visible tones per tile against 12 and 10 for the references, 0% near-flat coverage, and 0% neutral dark edges, so the outlines carry a tint (dark red-brown beside the red posts). The craft is still shallower than the references. The red posts and tie beam have only about 2-3 steps (base red, one highlight, one dark side), and the black kasagi cap is close to a single dark tone with a thin highlight. The grey stone bases have 2-3 tones and no per-stone shading. The houses show 5-6 steps per material, with per-tile scallop highlights, plaster speckle and stone-by-stone shading. Nothing like that grain or speckle appears on the posts or beams, which read as smooth, simple, slightly sticker-like surfaces. A careful artist would see it as thinner and flatter than the references, and when in doubt it fails.

The nuki and shimaki beams are drawn as front-facing strips, which is normal for this subject. The stone bases have a light top strip at rows 26-27 above a darker front. There is no isometric side face.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate is a small torii gate, not a whole building with roof, walls and door, so it does not match the reference kind. It is a thin, sparse object, so the measured tiles are not a fair basis. By eye, the red pillars and beams show about 3 lightness steps (highlight, mid red, dark red), against 5-6 steps on the reference roof tiles and walls. The outline is a dark red-brown tint, and the measured 0% neutral edge share supports that, so it is not a black sticker line. The grey stone bases are simple with little per-stone grain, and the red surfaces have no tile scallops or grain. Visible tones per tile (11) are on par with the references (10 and 12), and near-flat coverage is 0%, so there are no large flat fills. Still, the shading is shallower and the texture thinner than the Beodeul pieces. A careful artist would find it a little flatter next to the references, and when in doubt it fails.

answer.evidence: The kasagi (the widest part, 48px) has a slate top band at rows 1-2. A lighter front-edge line at row 3 follows, then dark eave shadow at rows 4-5. This gives a roof top surface of about 3 rows above the front faces. The red beams and pillars (rows 7-30) form a front face of well over 3 rows, with highlight and shadow shading and no side face. The stone bases have only a slight lighter top at rows 24-25. The roof top is thin, but it is a real top band with an edge line and shadow, not a rim alone.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate is a small, thin torii prop compared against whole houses, so I judged it by eye and by the measured facts. It has 11 visible tones per 16x16 tile, against 12 and 10 in the references. Near-flat coverage is 0%, the same as both references. The dark edge pixels are 0% near-neutral, so the outlines lean red or brown beside the red wood and are not a black sticker line. The red pillars and crossbeams, the dark kasagi cap and the grey stone bases each show a few separate value steps, and no large area is a single flat colour. The ramps (about 4 steps) are shallower than the roof-tile ramps in the references (5-6 steps) and the piece has less fine grain. That is expected for a thin gate with no tile or plaster surfaces. A careful artist would accept it next to the references without it looking flat or sticker-like. The call is a borderline pass.
